title: AI Data Centers Are Overheating — Massive Cooling Failures Threaten the AI Boom
description:
AI is growing faster than the world can cool it — and today’s data centers are feeling the heat. From high-profile outages to billion-dollar cooling investments, the infrastructure behind AI is now facing its biggest technical challenge: keeping servers cool enough to stay online.

In this video, we break down:
✔ Why AI and cloud servers are overheating
✔ The cooling failure that halted CME Group trading
✔ How liquid cooling is becoming the new industry standard
✔ Billion-dollar acquisitions reshaping the data-center market
✔ What this means for investors, tech companies, and the future of AI infrastructure

With AI workloads exploding, cooling tech is now one of the most important — and profitable — parts of the industry.

If you follow U.S. business news, AI trends, big tech, or market-moving infrastructure developments, this is a story you don’t want to miss.

Subscribe to MarketPulse News for daily U.S. business updates!

#AIBusiness #DataCenters #CoolingTech #TechNews #USBusinessNews #AIInfrastructure #MarketPulseNews #CloudComputing #AIGrowth #TechInvesting
transcript: Breaking news from Market Pulse. The fastest way to stay ahead in business world. AI servers are cooking the planet and data centers are scrambling to keep things cool. The global rush to build more data centers driven by surging demand for cloud storage and power hungry. AI workloads is sparking a hidden crisis. Overheating. Just this week, trading at CME Group, the world's largest exchange operator, ground to a halt. The culprit, a data center near Chicago, run by Cyrus 1, experienced a cooling failure. Suddenly, the spotlight is on what many in tech already feared. Heat, not just computation, might be the AI era's biggest bottleneck. While data centers are overheating, AI and cloud servers draw enormous power, and that power produces intense heat. In tightly packed server wrecks, air conditioning and traditional cooling simply aren't enough to dissipate the heat generated by modern AI workloads. If server chips overheat, they can malfunction or shut down, which means downtime, lost revenue, and shaken trust from clients from air to liquid. How cooling is evolving. To fight this heat challenge, data center operators are increasingly turning to liquid cooling. A method up to 3,000 times more effective than traditional air cooling. But swapping air fans for water or coolant lines isn't plug-andplay. Liquid cooling introduces new risks, leaks, corrosion, and water usage concerns, and requires specific infrastructure and maintenance regimes. Some big players are already experimenting with more advanced systems. For instance, closed loop cooling designs where water circulates continuously without needing constant fresh supply. Promised to reduce both water consumption and thermal risk. Some data centers are also exploring heat reuse using waste heat from servers for heating buildings or other systems. Quietly turning a problem into a potential sustainability win. Big money is now flowing into cooling infrastructure. Because cooling now represents up to 40% of a data cent's total energy use, the demand for efficient cooling solutions is fueling a wave of big deals. Eaton is in the process of buying the thermal division business of Boyd Corporation for roughly $9.5 billion clearly positioning itself to supply nextgen cooling tech. Meanwhile, Vertive, another big name in data center infrastructure, has announced a $1 billion acquisition of Purge intermediate to expand its liquid cooling services. That means cooling systems are no longer just a support cost. They're rapidly becoming major business and investment opportunities. What this means for AI and investors watching the space, infrastructure matters more than ever. As AI workloads grow, the success of cloud giants won't just depend on chips or software, but on whether they can manage heat, power, and sustainability at massive scale. Cooling is now a distinct investment sector. Firms that build and supply nextg cooling solutions could see major upside as demand explodes. What do you think? Drop your thoughts below. Thanks for watching. This is Market Pulse News. Like, share, and subscribe for more.

title: FLASHCARDS! How You Can Reduce AI Energy Use

While AI is revolutionizing our world, it comes with a hidden cost, massive energy consumption and increasing strain on our planet. In this episode, you’ll learn how data centers contribute to global electricity use, how your everyday digital habits add to the problem, and most importantly, what you can do to help curb energy consumption. From holding tech companies accountable to making smarter personal choices, this episode empowers you to take meaningful action toward a more sustainable digital future.

   What You’ll Learn in This Episode  How AI and data centers contribute to global energy consumption and carbon emissions Simple, practical ways to reduce your personal digital energy footprint How to advocate for sustainable technology and hold companies accountable    Key Takeaways  Data centers already consume ~1% of global electricity, and demand is rising rapidly Everyday actions like sending emails, streaming, and using AI tools all have an energy cost Small habit changes can collectively make a significant environmental impact  Consumer pressure and policy advocacy can push tech companies toward sustainability   

   Call to Action   Audit your digital habits today: Clean out your inbox, reduce unnecessary emails, and limit high-energy digital activities  Support sustainable companies: Choose tech platforms committed

forums, and, yes, public posts from social media.  So if you’ve ever posted something online under 
your real name or a trackable username, there’s   a chance it’s already part of a model’s “memory.” 
. Once training’s done, that data is locked in,   and it can’t magically learn new facts unless 
someone retrains it. It also can’t forget them.  On their own, these two are harmless. They’re 
just processing whatever you feed them.  The problem shows up when you add agents, 
those background programs we just talked   about. They collect your personal data, bundle 
it with your request, and feed it to the AI.  Finally, you’ve got the NPU, the 
Neural Processing Unit. Sounds intense,   but it’s just a chip that makes the math faster. 
It’s not storing anything or spying on you — it’s   basically a calculator on steroids.
So remember: AI is just software   plus a model. It’s the agents you add 
that turn it into a privacy problem.  The Agent Problem: How AI Actually Spies
Here’s where things go from “interesting   tech” to “privacy nightmare.”
Agents are personal assistants   you never hired, and they don’t work for you.
Take Windows Recall — it quietly takes screenshots   of your activity, runs them through AI for 
analysis, and stores the results for later.  Or Apple’s media analysis daemon — it 
scans new files or photos, has the AI   evaluate them, then saves that information.
Some browser-based AI assistants go further,   grabbing full page content, sometimes 
even what you type into forms,   and shipping it off to a server.
The pattern’s the same every time:  1. Agent collects the data.
2. AI processes it.  3. Agent stores or sends it somewhere else.
Do it once and you’ve got a snapshot of a   moment. Do it all the time and you’ve basically 
got a running diary of someone’s virtual life. And if you think this kind of spying is 
unique to AI, you’re in for a surprise.   We’ve seen the same kind of silent tracking 
buried in apps and devices for years,   and here’s the full breakdown in this video
Some AI runs entirely on your device. That’s   local AI — it processes what you give it and 
doesn’t send anything out unless you tell it to.  And if you firewall it or keep 
it offline, it stays in its box. Then there’s cloud AI, the kind that 
lives on someone else’s servers.  Your request, and often the context attached 
to it, is sent out for processing. That’s   where logging, storage, and “service 
improvement” suddenly come into play. Local, open-source models are 
generally safer because you   can see exactly what’s running 
and cut off outside connections. Cloud AI can be safe too, but only 
if you control the data you feed it.  Skip anything personal, avoid 
giving it your full digital history,   and don’t assume “private” in the 
marketing means private in reality. The key difference is control. 
With local AI, you hold it.  But with cloud AI, you’re trusting 
someone else to handle it and   hoping they live up to their privacy promises.
If you control the tech, you control the data —   and that means AI runs on your terms, not theirs.
